concepts.name: ECB: Definition, Scope and Instruments
key_dimensions: What qualifies as ECB vs. what is excluded (e.g., trade credit, FDI, FPI)
Instruments covered: loans, bonds, debentures, preference shares, FCCB, FCEB
Distinction between ECB and Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs) vs. Foreign Currency Exchangeable Bonds (FCEBs)
UPSC trap: Not all foreign borrowings are ECBs — trade credits and NRI deposits are outside ECB framework

concepts.name: ECB Regulatory Framework: RBI vs. Government of India roles
key_dimensions: Legal basis: FEMA 1999 and RBI's Master Directions on ECB
RBI's role as regulator vs. Ministry of Finance's role in policy formulation
Automatic Route vs. Approval Route — who decides, thresholds, and eligible sectors
UPSC trap: Confusion between RBI 'automatic route' approval and FIPB/DPIIT approval for FDI

concepts.name: ECB Tracks: Track I, Track II, and Track III Framework
key_dimensions: Track I: Medium-term foreign currency ECBs for permissible end-uses
Track II: Long-term foreign currency ECBs with more liberal end-uses
Track III: Indian Rupee-denominated ECBs (Masala Bonds fall here)
UPSC trap: After 2019 rationalization, RBI merged into two categories — FCY ECB and INR ECB — older track nomenclature is a common trap

concepts.name: Eligible Borrowers and Lenders under ECB
key_dimensions: Eligible borrowers: corporates, PSUs, NBFCs, microfinance institutions, startups (with conditions)
Eligible lenders: foreign equity holders, international banks, capital markets, export credit agencies, multilateral institutions
Restrictions: Individuals and entities in FATF non-compliant countries cannot be lenders
UPSC trap: Not all companies can borrow under automatic route — minimum average maturity and sector restrictions apply

concepts.name: ECB End-Use Restrictions and Negative List
key_dimensions: Permitted end-uses: capital expenditure, import of capital goods, infrastructure, working capital (limited)
Negative list: Real estate (residential), equity investment, on-lending to subprime segments, purchase of land
Recent relaxation: Real estate affordable housing was allowed as an exception
UPSC trap: Working capital is NOT freely permitted — only infrastructure and export sectors have relaxed rules

concepts.name: Minimum Average Maturity Period (MAMP) for ECB
key_dimensions: General MAMP: 3 years for ECB up to USD 50 million; 5 years for amounts beyond
Exceptions: Infrastructure, manufacturing sectors may have different MAMP requirements
Masala Bonds have a minimum maturity of 3 years
UPSC trap: MAMP is not the same as loan tenure — it is the weighted average maturity obligation

concepts.name: All-in-Cost Ceiling for ECBs
key_dimensions: Definition: Total cost including interest rate, fees, charges — expressed as spread over benchmark rate
Benchmark rates: LIBOR (phased out) replaced by SOFR/Term SOFR; RBI adjusts ceilings periodically
Rationale: Prevents excessively costly foreign borrowing that increases debt servicing burden
UPSC trap: LIBOR discontinuation and transition to SOFR is a live regulatory issue; RBI issued revised guidelines

concepts.name: Masala Bonds: INR-denominated ECBs
key_dimensions: Definition: Rupee-denominated bonds issued overseas — currency risk borne by foreign investor, not borrower
Key issuers: HDFC, NTPC, NHAI; listed on London Stock Exchange and Singapore Exchange
Regulatory framework: Part of Track III ECB; listed under RBI's ECB Master Direction
UPSC trap: Masala Bonds reduce currency risk for Indian issuers unlike regular FCY ECBs — this distinction is frequently tested

concepts.name: Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs)
key_dimensions: Structure: Bonds issued in foreign currency, convertible into equity at a predetermined price
Currency risk lies with the Indian company until conversion; if not converted, repayment in FCY
Regulatory treatment: Treated as ECB until conversion, then as FDI post-conversion
UPSC trap: FCCBs occupy an overlap between ECB and FDI — pre-conversion vs. post-conversion regulatory treatment is a classic trap

concepts.name: ECB and Hedging Requirements
key_dimensions: Mandatory hedging: Infrastructure companies borrowing above certain thresholds must hedge 70% of exposure
Natural hedge concept: Export earnings serving as a hedge for ECB repayments
RBI's concerns: Unhedged Foreign Currency Exposure (UFCE) leads to systemic risk
UPSC trap: Hedging mandates apply selectively — not all ECB borrowers face the same hedging obligation

concepts.name: ECB and Capital Account Convertibility
key_dimensions: ECB is a capital account transaction under FEMA — governed by Schedule I of FEMA (Capital Account Regulations)
India has partial capital account convertibility — ECB is a controlled but facilitated inflow
Tarapore Committee recommendations on full capital account convertibility and ECB liberalization
UPSC trap: Current account is fully convertible; capital account is NOT — ECB sits under the controlled capital account regime

concepts.name: ECB Proceeds: Parking and Utilization Rules
key_dimensions: Proceeds parked abroad must be in permitted instruments: deposits with banks, Treasury bills, money market instruments
Proceeds remitted to India: credited to borrower's account and used only for specified end-uses
ECB proceeds cannot be used for capital market investments or for routing to subsidiary companies freely
UPSC trap: Parking rules differ between 'proceeds kept abroad' vs. 'proceeds brought to India' — two distinct compliance regimes

concepts.name: Macroeconomic Implications of ECBs: Benefits vs. Risks
key_dimensions: Benefits: Supplements domestic savings, lower global interest rates, access to long-term capital, forex inflows
Risks: Exchange rate risk, external debt sustainability, sudden stops in capital flows, balance of payment vulnerability
India's external debt composition: ECBs constitute the largest share of India's external debt
UPSC trap: ECB inflows improve BoP capital account but excessive ECB raises external debt-to-GDP ratio concerns

concepts.name: ECB Limits and Liberalized ECB Framework (Post-2019 Rationalization)
key_dimensions: 2019 rationalization: Replaced 3-track with 2-framework (FCY ECB and INR ECB)
Raised automatic route limit to USD 750 million per financial year per entity
Expanded eligible borrowers to include HFCs, port trusts, units in SEZs
UPSC trap: The revised framework significantly liberalized end-use restrictions compared to the earlier strict framework — 'before and after' comparison is examinable

concepts.name: ECB vs. Trade Credit: Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: Trade credit: Short-term foreign borrowing for import of goods/services — maturity up to 3 years
ECB: Broader instrument not tied specifically to import transactions; longer maturity
Regulatory treatment: Trade credit governed separately under RBI's Trade Credit framework, not ECB Master Direction
UPSC trap: Both are foreign borrowings and affect external debt, but trade credit is NOT classified as ECB — frequently confused

concepts.name: Offshore Rupee Market and ECB: Linkage
key_dimensions: Masala Bonds create an offshore INR market, supporting rupee internationalization
RBI's cautious stance: Offshore INR market can affect onshore exchange rate and monetary policy transmission
Linkage to GIFT City (IFSC): ECBs can be raised through GIFT City with different regulatory treatment
UPSC trap: GIFT IFSC-based ECBs have a distinct regulatory regime — entities in IFSC are treated as non-residents for ECB purposes

concepts.name: ECB and Infrastructure Financing: Special Provisions
key_dimensions: Infrastructure sector: Relaxed end-use norms, longer MAMP eligibility, higher limits under automatic route
Permitted borrowers: NHAI, power companies, telecom, ports — even SPVs for infrastructure projects
ECB for refinancing Rupee loans: Permitted specifically for infrastructure — reduces domestic bank credit pressure
UPSC trap: Infrastructure is the only sector where ECB can be used to refinance existing rupee loans — this is an exception, not the rule

concepts.name: Default, Restructuring and Reporting Obligations under ECB
key_dimensions: Reporting: Borrowers must file Loan Registration Number (LRN) application; monthly reporting via ECB-2 returns
Loan Registration Number (LRN): Mandatory before drawdown — issued by RBI's DSIM department
Restructuring: Any change in ECB terms (maturity, cost, lender) requires RBI approval
UPSC trap: LRN is a pre-condition for ECB drawdown — non-reporting is a FEMA violation, not just a procedural lapse

concepts.name: Startups and ECBs: Special Window
key_dimensions: Startups recognized under DPIIT can raise ECB under a special framework with relaxed norms
Allowed for all purposes except real estate and financial products; can use for working capital (exception to general rule)
Minimum average maturity: 3 years; lenders can include foreign venture capital investors
UPSC trap: Startups are one of the few categories where ECB for working capital is explicitly permitted — a deliberate exception to the standard negative list

concepts.name: External Debt Sustainability and ECB Policy Calibration
key_dimensions: India's external debt indicators: Debt-to-GDP ratio, debt service ratio, short-term debt to forex reserves ratio
RBI periodically tightens or relaxes ECB norms based on macroeconomic conditions (e.g., tightening during INR depreciation episodes)
Borrow-and-hedge vs. borrow-and-expose: Policy tension between encouraging ECB inflows and managing systemic forex risk
UPSC trap: RBI uses ECB policy as a macro-prudential tool — when rupee is under pressure, RBI has historically tightened ECB norms rather than liberalized them
